notes:
These are verse-by-verse notes on Hebrews 5. Each point gives its source page. At the end is a list of what I couldn't find.

---

**v. 1**
- Ellicott: "gifts" set beside "sacrifices" means the bloodless offerings of the Law. He thinks the writer has the Day of Atonement in mind, when all offerings, as well as all sacrifices, had relation to "sins." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/hebrews/5.htm
- Guzik: not every sacrifice offered a blood atonement for sin. Many of the ritual sacrifices were intended as simple gifts to God, expressing thanks and desiring fellowship. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hebrews-5/
- Wesley: the high priest stands between both sides, to bring God near to men, and men to God. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/hebrews-5.html
- Matthew Henry's application: let us never attempt to go to God but through Christ. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Hbr/Hbr_005.cfm
- Precept Austin: a priest has to be taken from among men to act for men. https://www.preceptaustin.org/hebrews_51-3

**v. 2**
- Ellicott: the word means to "deal gently with". A priest who didn't care, or who was too harsh, would be unfit to represent people. The wording leaves out sinning "with a high hand." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/hebrews/5.htm
- Light of Israel Commentary: the high priest dealt with sins of ignorance. Deliberate, "high-handed" sins meant being cut off from Israel's congregation (Numbers 15:30). https://www.studylight.org/commentary/hebrews/5-1.html
- Wesley: "compassion" means in proportion to the offence: so the Greek word signifies. The "weakness" is sinful weakness, so the priest needs the same mercy he shows. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/hebrews-5.html
- Gill: this is weakness of mind as well as body, "sinful infirmity." He compares it to Joshua the high priest's filthy clothes (Zechariah 3:3). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/hebrews-5.html
- Precept Austin: the priest should neither shrug off sin nor be harsh with sinners who repent. P. E. Hughes takes the weakness to come from human depravity, not just human nature. https://www.preceptaustin.org/hebrews_51-3

**v. 3**
- Ellicott: on the Day of Atonement the high priest offered a bullock and a ram for himself, and he confessed his own sins before the people's. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/hebrews/5.htm
- Gill: in this Christ differed from the high priest, for he had no sin of his own to offer for, Hebrews 7:27. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/hebrews-5.html
- Pink lists the contrasts: Aaron offered many sacrifices, Christ one. Aaron offered for his own sins, Christ was sinless. Aaron offered something outside himself, Christ offered himself. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/awp/hebrews-5.html

**v. 4**
- Guzik: the high priest came from God's people but was chosen by God, not by them. It was not an office to campaign for. He applies this today: thinking we can approach God without a priest is arrogance, but it is also great superstition to think we need any priest other than Jesus Christ Himself. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hebrews-5/
- Wesley: Aaron did not preach at all; preaching being no part of the priestly office. This touches on whether v. 4 applies to calls to ministry. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/hebrews-5.html
- Ellicott (on the Greek text): read "when he is called." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/hebrews/5.htm

**v. 5**
- Ellicott: in the Law of Moses the high priest is called "the anointed priest." So the title "the Christ" (the Anointed One) holds together both quotations: King and Son (Psalm 2:7) and Priest (Psalm 110:4). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/hebrews/5.htm
- What "today I have become Your Father" refers to is read differently:
  - Guzik: This refers to Jesus' resurrection from the dead. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hebrews-5/
  - Wesley: the call came from the One who said these words, but not, indeed, at the same time; for his generation was from eternity. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/hebrews-5.html
  - Gill: the words don't create Christ's priesthood. They describe the Father–Son relationship that made the Son fit for the office. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/hebrews/5.htm
- Gill: being made priest was an honour to Christ as man, not as God, to whose glory nothing can be added. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/hebrews/5.htm
- The Gospel Coalition: Psalms 2 and 110 are put side by side to show God himself appointed Christ priest. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/commentary/hebrews/

**v. 6**
- Ellicott: Psalm 110:4 is "the kernel" of the psalm and the theme of much of the letter, especially chapter 7. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/hebrews/5.htm
- Guzik: no high priest from Aaron's line ever had a priesthood "forever". https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hebrews-5/
- Barnes: the verse says "priest," not "high priest," because Melchizedek did not bear that title. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/hebrews/5-6.html
- Constable, quoting Morris: there was no succession of priests from Melchizedek and thus no 'order.' https://www.studylight.org/commentary/hebrews/5-6.html
- **Catholic view:** Tom Nash reasons that a priest offers sacrifices (v. 1), and Melchizedek brought bread and wine. So "the order of Melchizedek" means Christ's one sacrifice made present under bread and wine in the Mass. https://www.catholic.com/magazine/online-edition/what-is-the-point-of-a-priest
  - Another Catholic Answers article cites Hahn and Mitch: Melchizedek's is the older family order of priesthood, before Aaron. https://www.catholic.com/magazine/online-edition/when-apostles-became-priests
  - Compare Guzik's point at v. 4 that we need no priest but Jesus.

**v. 7** (the most debated verse)
- **Gethsemane or the cross?**
  - Wesley and Guzik point to the garden. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/hebrews-5.html and https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hebrews-5/
  - Ellicott: the "loud cry" points to the crucifixion and Psalm 22, and both events are probably meant. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/hebrews/5.htm
- **"Offered":** Ellicott says this is a sacrifice word in Hebrews. So the prayers were part of the sacrifice that made up his whole life and death. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/hebrews/5.htm
- **"Save from death":** several writers say the prayer was answered by the resurrection, not by escaping death.
  - Ellicott and Wuest: the Greek means "out of death," not "from" it. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/hebrews/5.htm and https://www.studylight.org/commentary/hebrews/5-9.html
  - Ligonier: Jesus still went to the cross, and His deliverance was His resurrection. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/the-prayers-and-suffering-of-jesus
- **"Heard because of His reverence": translators really differ here.**
  - Ellicott prefers the reading of all the Greek Fathers, heard *for his reverent fear*. He contrasts it with the rendering that came into the 1611 KJV through Calvin and Beza ("heard in that he feared"). The word means a careful, forward-looking fear, not terror. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/hebrews/5.htm
  - Barnes lists the options. Beza: "delivered from fear." Luther: heard because he had God in reverence. Barnes himself takes "reverence." https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/bsb/hebrews/5-7.html
  - Calvin's view, as summarised by Pink: what Christ feared was God's judgment on our sins. Pink thinks the two readings should be combined. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/awp/hebrews-5.html
  - Ligonier quotes Calvin: Jesus dreaded not death itself but God's judgment seat. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/the-prayers-and-suffering-of-jesus
  - Wesley: he was heard in what he most feared, the weight of God's justice. The cup didn't pass, but he drank it without any fear. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/hebrews-5.html
- **Application:** Matthew Henry says it sets us an example of fervent prayer: How many dry prayers, how few wet ones. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Hbr/Hbr_005.cfm

**v. 8**
- Ellicott quotes Lünemann: Jesus already had the will to obey. Suffering turned that will into actual deeds. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/hebrews/5.htm
- Guzik: Jesus didn't move from disobedience to obedience, or learn *how* to obey. He learned the *experience* of obeying. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hebrews-5/
- Matthew Henry: he never performed a greater act of obedience than dying on the cross. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Hbr/Hbr_005.cfm
- Wesley: "Son" is added so no one is put off by his weakness. It also shows his sonship did not arise merely from his resurrection. This is another contrast with Guzik's reading at v. 5. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/hebrews-5.html
- **A popular teaching rejected:** Guzik answers those who say learning through suffering is only God's "second best" and that God means us to learn only from his word: Jesus was never in the Father's second best. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hebrews-5/
  - Gill says something similar: being God's child doesn't exempt anyone from suffering. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/hebrews/5.htm

**v. 9**
- **"Made perfect":** The Gospel Coalition notes that in the Greek Old Testament this word is used for consecrating priests to enter God's holy place. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/commentary/hebrews/
  - Matthew Henry: it means he completed the earthly part of his work as a perfect atoning sacrifice. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Hbr/Hbr_005.cfm
- **"Eternal":** Ellicott says the salvation is eternal because he is a priest "forever". https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/hebrews/5.htm
- **"All who obey Him": how faith and obedience fit together is stressed differently.**
  - Gill: Christ brings everyone he saves to obey him, though their obedience is no cause of their salvation; Christ himself is the alone author of that. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/hebrews-5.html
  - Matthew Henry: salvation is actually bestowed on none but those who obey Christ. Knowing the doctrine or professing faith isn't enough. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Hbr/Hbr_005.cfm
  - Wesley: obeying means doing and suffering his whole will. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/hebrews-5.html
  - Ligonier puts it as salvation for all who trust in him alone. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/the-prayers-and-suffering-of-jesus

**v. 10**
- Ellicott: the word means "addressed." "Priest" becomes "high priest," which brings out the psalm's full meaning. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/hebrews/5.htm
- Wesley: the word means "surnamed." He thinks the Holy Spirit kept Melchizedek's identity hidden so he would be a clearer picture of Christ. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/hebrews-5.html
- Gill: Christ is the source of eternal salvation because he is a priest forever. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/hebrews/5.htm
- Catholic view: Nash calls vv. 7–10 the most profound passage in the biblical story of the Mass. https://www.catholic.com/magazine/online-edition/what-is-the-point-of-a-priest

**v. 11**
- Ellicott: the readers have *become* sluggish. Once they had sharp hearing; now they have lost interest, and with it the ability to take things in. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/hebrews/5.htm
- Guzik: "dull of hearing" is a heart problem, not an ear problem. The dullness usually comes before the wish to give up. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hebrews-5/
- Wesley: the difficulty comes less from the subject than from the readers' laziness. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/hebrews-5.html
- Gill gives possible causes: sluggishness, pride, prejudice, and the cares of life. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/hebrews-5.html

**v. 12**
- Gill: the readers had had about thirty years since Pentecost. "Oracles of God" means the Scriptures. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/hebrews/5.htm
- Wesley: the "first principles" are the ones listed in Hebrews 6:1. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/hebrews-5.html
- Matthew Henry: From those to whom much is given much is expected. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Hbr/Hbr_005.cfm

**v. 13 and v. 14: the clearest disagreement between Protestant traditions**
- **Wesley (Methodist):**
  - "Milk" is the simplest doctrines. The immature include all who desire and can digest nothing but the doctrine of justification and imputed righteousness.
  - The "solid food" is the deeper truths about "perfection" (6:1).
  - https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/hebrews-5.html
- **Gill:**
  - The "message of righteousness" is the gospel of Christ's own righteousness, which strips a person of their own.
  - The "maturity" of v. 14 is maturity of knowledge, not holiness: there is no perfection of holiness but in Christ, and all believers fall short in this life.
  - https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/hebrews/5.htm
- **Matthew Henry:** we have spiritual senses, damaged by sin but restored by grace, and they grow stronger with use. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Hbr/Hbr_005.cfm

---

**What I couldn't find**

I ran out of search and page-fetch calls before covering everything. I found nothing on:
- Lutheran sources from lcms.org or 1517.org (the only Luther point is Barnes's note at v. 7)
- Pentecostal or charismatic sources other than Guzik
- Orthodox sources (oca.org)
- netbible.org or bibleodyssey.org scholarship
- the Pulpit Commentary
- any page naming prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching on this chapter

I only partly read Guzik's notes on vv. 12–14 and Ellicott's on v. 12 onward.
